title: Quantum mechanics from competing formalisms to a shared predictive framework
pressure: Old quantum theory explained selected spectra but failed as a coherent general method for multi-electron atoms, intensities, scattering and increasingly rich atomic measurements.
preExistingWorldModel: Planck, Einstein and Bohr had established quantization ideas, while spectroscopy and atomic experiments produced constraints that the older orbital picture could not consistently satisfy.
candidateRoutes: Heisenberg matrix mechanics based on observable transitions
de Broglie matter waves and Schrödinger wave mechanics
retain classical hidden mechanism until a more intuitive model appears
observationsAndInstruments: Schrödinger produced wave mechanics in 1926 from a different starting representation.
The approaches were shown to yield equivalent predictions despite different mathematical forms.
Born introduced a probabilistic reading of the wavefunction; Dirac generalized the formalism and incorporated relativity for the electron.
Electron diffraction and Compton scattering connected the new formalisms to materially different experiments.
decisiveTests: A new formalism had to reproduce existing spectral results and succeed on cases where old quantum theory failed.
Equivalent numerical predictions from different representations tested whether surface mathematical language or invariant consequence should dominate.
Relativistic extension created new predictions such as antiparticle structure rather than only curve-fitting old spectra.
technicalOrScientificTransition: Quantum theory moved from semi-classical patchwork to general mathematical formalisms whose empirical success did not require one shared intuitive picture of microscopic reality.
rivalsAndFailures: Interpretational disagreement persisted despite predictive convergence.
Competing formalisms initially looked ontologically different.
Not every mathematical extension was equally tractable computationally.
The success of quantum mechanics did not make measurement/interpretation disputes disappear.
diffusionAndScaling: The framework rapidly reorganized atomic, molecular, solid-state and nuclear physics and created reusable calculation methods.
standardsAndInstitutions: Göttingen, Copenhagen, Zurich, Cambridge and international scientific exchange formed a distributed research network rather than one laboratory pipeline.
externalitiesAndCorrections: Later military/nuclear uses created consequences far outside the initial atomic-spectra research objective.
secondOrderEffects: Quantum formalism expanded the set of calculable/predictable phenomena and generated new experimental questions and instrumentation demands.
sourceNativeSummary: The historical transition is not one representation defeating all others: materially different mathematical representations converged on shared predictive content while interpretational ontology remained open.
unresolvedHistoricalQuestions: How much equivalence was recognized immediately versus retrospectively normalized in textbooks?
Which interpretational disputes materially changed experimental choices during 1925–30?
